title: Five hundred and fifty years of Nanak
word: Five hundred and fifty years of Nanak
hook: Sikhs and others mark Guru Nanak's birth with celebrations around the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Granth became Guru, and your line was the eternal guru. Did a hukamnama go with you into a choice? Today the counting reaches all the way back, to the first Guru's birth. Day one thousand twenty-five.

At dusk, the strings of small lights along a gurdwara roof blink on. Clay lamps lined up on a wall. A procession moving through a city street, the Guru Granth Sahib carried on a decorated float, people sweeping the road clean in front of it, and someone handing out sweets at the corner. It looks like a festival of light, and it is one. It's Guru Nanak's gurpurab, the celebration of his birth. When the count reached a round number, the lights went up in Punjab and far beyond it. Today: five hundred and fifty years of Nanak.
screen: `LIGHTS ON A GURDWARA ROOF.` → `SWEEPING THE ROAD AHEAD.` → `GURU NANAK'S GURPURAB.`

segments.voice: First, the celebration. A gurpurab is a Guru's day. For Guru Nanak's, Sikhs hold an akhand path, an unbroken reading of the whole Guru Granth Sahib, ending on the day itself. There are nagar kirtans in the streets, langar for anyone, and lights in the evening. Second, why light. Bhai Gurdas, in his first var, describes Nanak's coming in a picture people still quote: the true Guru Nanak appeared, the mist cleared, and light spread through the world. The lamps on the gurdwara roof are that line, made visible. Third, what scholars notice. The gurpurab is celebrated at the full moon of the month of Kartik, in autumn. Some early accounts of his life place his birth in a different month, in spring, and historians have discussed the difference. Sikh practice keeps the celebration where it is, and both conversations go on side by side. Fourth, the round number. A count like five hundred and fifty is just arithmetic. What makes it matter is what people do with it. When that count came, Sikhs and others marked it with kirtan, langar, lights, and service, in villages and in cities across the world. The day wasn't about how long ago Nanak lived. It was about whether his light is still spreading. That's today's line: five hundred fifty years.
screen: `A GURU'S DAY.` · `THE MIST CLEARED, LIGHT SPREAD.` · `KARTIK, OR SPRING?` · `WHAT PEOPLE DO WITH A NUMBER.` · then, large: `FIVE HUNDRED FIFTY YEARS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes to clear a road. In the procession, people sweep the street before the Guru Granth Sahib passes. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one person with a hard road just ahead: an exam, a hospital visit, a new job, a long goodbye. Breathe in, and see the road in front of them. Breathe out, and picture clearing one thing from it: a worry, a chore, a stone. Do that for a few breaths. Then name one real thing you could clear for them this week. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Five hundred and fifty years of Nanak. The round-number gurpurab of Guru Nanak's birth, marked with akhand path, nagar kirtan, langar and lights around the world. Today's word.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED AND FIFTY YEARS OF NANAK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: five hundred fifty years. Today, light a lamp for Nanak, or for someone who brought light to you, and leave it burning safely for a while. Day one thousand twenty-five.

screen: `DAY 1025 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SIKHS IN PUBLIC LIFE ABROAD.`
